title: Start with the big things (I.5–I.8)
hookLine: first clear away serious sin, then the smaller attachments
tomorrow: why are you here at all? a bishop's first answer

lines: THE TIME OF PRUNING IS COME.
cards: Cleaning out a garage, you don't start by dusting a shelf while a broken couch blocks the door. Too much to fix, and where do you even start?
Francis de Sales opens the work of change with a line from the Song of Songs, in the Douay-Rheims: "The flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning is come."
The flowers, he says, are the good desires already budding. The pruning is what has to go so they can grow.

teach.b: Pruning has an order, and de Sales lays it out. It starts slow, like dawn. Change usually comes little by little, he says, the way morning grows into day.
Some people have been changed in a moment, but that's not the ordinary road, so he asks for patience, and courage, with yourself.

Then the big things first. The first cleansing is from serious sin, what Catholics call mortal sin, and for that he points to confession, recommending a general confession that looks honestly over a whole life.
Then the roots. The second cleansing goes deeper: not just the sin, but the fondness for it. He remembers the Israelites in the desert, free of Egypt and still missing its food.
A person can leave a wrong behind and still look back at it with longing.
Here's the image to keep: clear the big stones first, then work the soil, then pull the small weeds.
Fussing over a weed while a boulder sits in the bed is wasted work.
So the answer to the hook is plain. Don't start with the easy little thing. Start with the couch in the doorway.

how: Catholics confess serious sins in the sacrament of confession; some make a general confession, looking back over their whole life, at a turning point such as a retreat or before marriage.

games.q: what does “start with the big things” mean?
o: a spring garden chore done before planting
change that clears serious things before small ones
a plan to fix every small habit in one week

games.q: the order of pruning — tap the pairs.
p: free of Egypt, missing its food

s: de Sales says real change always happens all at once
it usually grows little by little, like morning into day.
de Sales says you can leave a sin and still be fond of it
like the Israelites, free of Egypt and still missing its food.
the smart start is the small, easy habits
big stones first, then the soil, then the small weeds.

games.q: your friend wants to get her life together: she's starting with a new planner and a skincare routine, while she still hasn't spoken to her sister in a year. what would de Sales point to?
o: the sister first; that's the stone blocking the bed.
the planner first; small wins build momentum.
everything at once, so nothing gets left behind.
games.why: clear the big stones first, then work the soil, then pull the weeds. the order matters more than the speed.

practice: Pick up something with real weight, a heavy book, a full water bottle, a bag, and hold it in one hand. Let it stand for one big thing you've been stepping around: a habit, a grudge, a conversation you haven't had.
Feel the weight, name the thing honestly to yourself, and then slowly set it down in front of you.

wordCard.voice: Start with the big things. De Sales's order for change: serious sin first, then the fondness for it, little by little, like dawn becoming day.

carryVoice: Your line: clear the ground. The flowers are already there, waiting for room. Rest well.
